source.text: Can I get you anything to drink? :
context: Hi, I'm George. I'll be your waiter this evening. Are you ready to order or do you need a few more minutes?
I'm ready now. I'd like the roast chicken and a side order of corn.
And would you like an appetizer before your meal? The soup of the day is our delicious tomato soup.
I'll pass on the soup, but I'd like a garden salad.
Can I get you anything to drink? :
Yes, I'd like a glass of iced tea.
Okay. I'll be back in a minute with your drink and salad.

review.adaptation: Use only this visible prompt and exact original reply. Attach the trailing colon to its original drink-offer question. It is punctuation, not an independent proposition. Preserve both the question mark and colon and do not use the later iced-tea answer.

source.text: My name is Rick Fields and of course, I am here, once again, with the man that seals the deal, Bob Copeland. '
context: Hello baseball fans, and welcome back to today's game! My name is Rick Fields and of course, I am here, once again, with the man that seals the deal, Bob Copeland. '
It's a beautiful day to see two world class teams face each other and fight for their right to be called champions.
Well, the national anthem has just been sung, and the umpire has started the game. It's time to play ball!
Roger Vargas is up at bat. The pitcher winds up and strike one!
A very nice curve ball by the pitcher. The catcher gives him the sign, he winds up and Vargas gets a line drive!
The players are scrambling to get the ball. Vargas gets to first base and he's still going! The outfielder throws it to second! Vargas slides! He's safe!
We have a runner on third and up at bat is Brian Okapi! There's the pitch, he hits it! It's going, going, that ball is gone!
Home run by Okapi! That puts this team ahead by two as we are at the bottom of the fifth inning here at Richie Stadium!

review.adaptation: Use only this visible prompt and exact original reply. Attach the detached terminal apostrophe to the preceding self-introduction. Preserve every character and treat the apostrophe as punctuation, not an independent utterance or evidence of missing speech.
